column9: rust I depicts an autonomous war machine that has fallen out of use, outlasting humanity and the war it was originally designed for. The machine has sunk into a pond where it has since rusted over and now feeds the local ecosystem, covered in lichens, barnacles, and mosses, taking on a new life after its first. While mankind is no longer present to witness this new turn of the cycle, its legacy lives on through the machines it created which in turn decay to give life to the local flora.

column16: silent spring I depicts an armed cannon riddled with arrows, having fallen in some unnamed battle. The title of the piece references Rachel Carson’s book of the same name which helped to shed light on the potential long-lasting impacts of synthetic pesticide use on the environment and the dangers it posed to life as a whole. In this piece, mankind has already fallen to a war of its own making, its weapons and nature itself outlasting humanity.

column9: This work is a materialist expression of contemporary existential anxiety. Each viewing is singular in that it significantly alters the celluloid and it's manipulations to a substantial degree and is accompanied by an improvised modular synthesizer performance.
column16: In Medias Res is a live stereoscopic projection event that employs shadow-play, live animation, and experimental projection techniques in an attempts to immerse the viewer deeply in impossible spaces and landscapes. Mechanized puppetry, video feedback and expanded cinema performances are displayed in anaglyphic 3D, working from techniques developed by the American Experimental Cinema pioneer Ken Jacobs.

column8: Birch hollow, field recording, audio transducer, custom electronics, brass
column9: A transducer converts energy from one form to another. Here, an audio voice coil excites the birch bark hollow, transforming it into a speaker membrane. Inspired by the haunting, descending call of the Veery, a migratory bird bridging Boreal/Mixed Hardwood and Amazon forests; Field recordings capture a chorus of forest dwellers: Swainson's Thrush, Magnolia Warbler, Cedar Waxwing, Black-and-white Warbler, Ovenbird, Black-throated Green Warbler, White-throated Sparrow, Red-eyed Vireo, Veery, Common Yellowthroat, Canada Warbler, Black-capped Chickadee, American Robin, Downy Woodpecker, Nashville Warbler, Red-winged Blackbird, and Pileated Woodpecker. Once still and quiet, the Birch bark now echoes the intricate harmonies of its environment.

Strup begins with a detective searching for clues in stories that may not belong to the person telling them. Set inside a memory-erasing machine, the experimental video essay explores addiction as a complex mechanism of emotional regulation and escape. Blurring the boundaries between substance use, dissociation, fantasy, and memory manipulation, Strup draws on optogenetic research into the alteration of memory.

This work is exploring the connection between violence and materialism, specifically in southern culture. Wrestling as a form of entertainment blurs the lines between theater and sport. There is an amalgamation of real and fake violence as well as real and fake personas that are put on display for the audience to take in. Peacocking and flashiness are coupled with this complex display of violence which intertwines these two ideas. This particular subject is only one example of the way that this phenomena can manifest in popular culture and American society. My work is centered around these themes of which I try to explore through my own lens of personal experience.

column9: “Snakes and Dungeons” is an interactive menu featuring projects created in 2026; it consists of a series of links, doors, windows, and interactive spaces hosted on a webpage—designed to be accessed via mobile phone or computer. All these links articulate, in one way or another, one or both of the two core themes of this moment and this generation: war and love. These two themes clash on the game board known as the world, intersecting within my own body to produce the "body" of work I present here. I invite you to share a few minutes of *extimacy*.

column9:
I built an account under the handle @thetoxicsludge_ to hold everything at once — memes, ideas, the smallest parts of an ordinary day — and watched it become something closer to an environment than a profile: its own weather, its own residents, its own rules for what got to survive. The platform is a kind of machine, and like any machine, it doesn't just hold what you put in — it reshapes you. What felt private got pulled outward, sorted, made visible or invisible by an algorithm deciding what was worth seeing. A playground started to function like a battlefield.

Turning the account into a physical object — mounting the collage on wood, packing it with hot glue — was an attempt to pull something back from that cycle. Glue and wood don't scroll away, and take real time and real pain to shape by hand. If the platform extracted a version of me and resold it as image, this object is the regeneration side of that same loop: something organic pushing back against something built to consume it. It doesn't undo the extraction. It just insists something human survives it.
